lines.note: Continues the preceding entry with kyuu-gyuu ga ichimoo, one hair from nine oxen. The scan restores the complete roman Japanese phrase after italic Vt; the Portuguese numerical complement follows on the next row.

runs.text: noue vacas. Item, Couſa muito pouca.

lines.note: Nove vacas completes the one-hair comparison, and the added sense is something extremely small in amount. This is running text continued from the preceding page, not a new headword.
Kyuujen is paraphrased by miya no mae, in front of the palace. Portuguese diante dos paços continues with the royal qualification below.
Reaes completes paços reaes, the royal palace. The short continuation is a separate physical row.

Kyuuji here denotes urgent business, explained by isogashii koto. The headword ends ji, not the provisional it; enlargement distinguishes the two tall s types in apreſſada from the beta-like sort in c1-l021.
Kyuuji is now old affairs or an old matter, explicitly furuqi coto. The Portuguese antigua confirms the distinction from the preceding urgent-business entry.

runs.text: O ſeruir, l, os que ſer-

lines.note: Kyuuji, explained by miyazukai, covers serving and those who serve. The italic alternative marker l belongs to the Portuguese apparatus; ser- continues below.
The continuation specifies service at table; kyuuji suru is translated as serving at table. Preserve the printed nasal abbreviation in uẽ and the separate example marker.
Kyuujin is miyabito, noble people of the court. The final co- begins the comparison como on the following row.
Completes como Cũgues, giving court nobles as the example. Cũgues is a Japanese title adapted within the Portuguese explanation, with its printed nasal abbreviation retained.
Kyuuin is equated with mimizu and Portuguese minhoca, an earthworm. The unusual-looking headword is coherent and is not repaired to the neighbouring kyuuji forms.
Kyuumei denotes an old bond or friendship, furuqi chigiri. The scan separates Furuqi and chiguiri; the upright S is a written-register label, outside the italic gloss.
This kyuumei is inquiry or investigation, explained by tadashi akiramuru. The full headword and its vowel mark are visible; Qimei was an OCR omission rather than a distinct entry.
Kyuumei suru means judging or examining. The scan joins the headword and supports Iulgar rather than Ialgar; Vt remains italic.
Kyuumin is explained by hinnin, poor people; the Portuguese additionally characterizes them as worn down. Its final des- belongs to desfeito below.
Feito completes desfeito, followed by canſado, exhausted. The example then begins kyuumin kodoku no, preparing the description of poor and solitary people below.
Tomogara completes the Japanese noun phrase for poor, solitary people. The damaged initial is t rather than OCR c; Portuguese ſoos has two o types, and deſ- continues into desemparados.
Emparados completes deſemparados, unsupported or abandoned. No new entry begins on this short continuation.
Kyuumon is rigorous questioning, tadashi too. The scan supports exame without the spurious r; the small mark over u is read as a caron rather than the provisional grave.

runs.text: ſe faz riguroſamente como dando tratos, &c.

lines.note: The examination is carried out rigorously, for example by applying torture. Tratos belongs to the historical interrogation gloss, not a neutral description of ordinary discussion.
Kyuuna describes something sudden or hurried. The double-s sort in apreßada is visibly beta-like, unlike the two tall s forms in c1-l005; this difference is retained.
Kyuuni is explicitly an adverb, glossed Derepente, suddenly. The printed one-word Portuguese spelling is retained.
Kyuunan is a sudden difficulty, niwakana nangi. Trabalho introduces hardship, with an alternative Portuguese gloss continuing below.
Perigo repentino completes the definition as sudden danger. The terminal S is upright and marks written usage rather than belonging to the italic explanation.
Kyuunen is a year of hardship, explained by kiwamaru toshi. The scan restores the headword and Qiuamaru and prints Anno with doubled n; the Portuguese adjective continues below.
Completes trabalhoso and gives a year of great famine as the example. The definition concerns hardship, not simply an old year.
The second kyuunen entry means old or former years, furuqi toshi. Annos has two n types; this entry is distinct from the preceding famine-year sense.
Paßados completes the alternative gloss, past years. The beta-like double-s sort is preserved as in the aligned draft.
Kyuunin is a person who receives a grant, tamawaru hito. The Portuguese begins a description of a man with an income; the scan corrects Honem to Homem.

runs.text: gũa renda do ſenhor pera o ſeruir.

lines.note: The income is received from a lord in return for service. Gũa completes algũa across the physical line break.
Qiuoo is an honoured elder, tattoqi okina. The headword reads Qiuô, without adding a length mark to u; voqina corrects the OCR voqiura.
The alternative describes an elderly, dignified person. The printed anciãa and peßoa are retained rather than modernized.
Kioi, kiou, kioota gives principal forms of the verb for taking courage or spirit. Portuguese ebrio is read as the closely set e brio, not as an adjective meaning drunken.
Gũa completes algũa, specifying help or favour as the source of renewed confidence. Historical fauor is retained.

runs.text: Eſforço, ou brio, que hum toma de

lines.note: Kioi is now the noun, renewed courage or spirit. The scan supplies the initial capital Q missing from the OCR; its gloss continues with de novo below.
Novo completes de novo, describing courage newly acquired. This short row belongs to the noun entry above.
Kioikakari, kakaru, kakatta means attacking after taking heart. Acometer and the printed separation de pois replace garbled OCR without regularizing the spacing.

runs.text: tomar animo com o bom ſucceßo, ou com al-

lines.note: The attacker is emboldened by success or some assistance. Enlargement supports ſucceßo rather than OCR ſuccepo; the upper arc of the double-s sort is broken, so its classification as ß remains a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.
Gũa ajuda completes the source of encouragement, some help. This closes the attack-after-encouragement definition.
Kyuuket is deciding a matter after inquiry, tadashi sadamuru. The headword retains final t, and the Japanese second verb begins with long ſ, not f.

runs.text: examinando concluir algũa couſa, ou dar ſẽ-

lines.note: Judging and examining lead to settling a matter or giving a sentence. The scan supports concluir, not conduir; ſẽ- is the abbreviated beginning of sentence continued below.
Tença completes the divided ſẽtença, judgment or sentence. The abbreviation is not expanded inside the transcription.
A separate kyuuket denotes the royal palace. The scan restores both the headword and Rey; the final period belongs with the italic Portuguese gloss.
Kyuuki concerns recording old matters, furuqi koto wo shirusu. Eſcritura corrects the damaged OCR and continues with its adjective below.
Antigua completes the description of an old writing or record. It is not part of the next law entry.
The repeated kyuuki is now an old law, furuqi nori. The scan supports the same headword spelling as above, but a distinct gloss.
Kyuukyuuna describes something sudden or accelerated. Both marked u vowels belong to the reduplicated headword; no extra j is visible.
Kyuuri is the native place or homeland, identified by furusato. The example begins kyuuri ni and continues with the verb of returning below; Patria corrects the OCR omission.
Cayeru completes kyuuri ni kaeru, returning to one's homeland. The Portuguese tornar à patria supplies the same motion and destination.
This kyuuri means the palace interior, miya no uchi. The scan supports Miyanovchi, including the n and positional v; the following row identifies whose palace is meant.
Dairi completes the Portuguese phrase about being within the imperial palace. It is a Japanese designation embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not a new headword.
Qiuri is the cucumber entry, distinguished from the preceding two by the unmarked u. Pipino is the printed Portuguese vegetable-name spelling.
Kyuusai is saving or rescue, explained by sukui and sukuu. The Japanese and Portuguese initial long-s letters were misread as f; ſal- continues into salvação below.
Uação completes ſaluação, salvation or rescue. Preserve the historical u/v spelling and the physical division of the word.
Kyuuso is a cornered rat, kiwamatta nezumi. The scan has doubled tt and the Portuguese beginning aßa-, which continues into assanhado rather than the OCR aganhado.

runs.text: nhado, ou que ſe ve em ſumo perigo. ¶

lines.note: Completes aßanhado and describes a rat in extreme danger. The Japanese proverb then begins again with kyuuso; the last o has no separate circumflex.

runs.text: O rato que ſe ve ja

lines.note: Kaette neko wo kamu completes the proverb: the cornered rat turns and bites the cat. The Portuguese visibly separates ve ja, meaning that it already sees itself in the desperate state described below.

runs.text: ſem remedio perſeguido, às vezes morde o ga-

lines.note: The rat is pursued with no escape and sometimes bites the cat. The final ga- belongs to Portuguese gato, continued below.

runs.text: to. Prouerb. Toma ſe em ſentido que os q̃ às

lines.note: To completes gato; Prouerb. explicitly labels the saying as a proverb. Its figurative interpretation begins here, and the abbreviated q̃ is retained without expansion.

runs.text: vezes desprezamos vendoſe em aperto, fazẽ

lines.note: Those whom we sometimes despise may retaliate when hard pressed. Enlarged comparison with neighbouring letter and word gaps supports continuous desprezamos rather than the OCR des prezamos.

runs.text: grande mal, ou matão aos mais valentes.

lines.note: The figurative explanation concludes that such people can badly harm, or kill, even the bravest. This completes the extended rat-and-cat proverb entry.
Kyuusoku is rest, directly glossed Descanſo. The compact single-line entry is separate from the house entry below.
Kyuutaku is an old house, furui ie. The scan prints Furui, not the malformed Furhi; pri- begins the comparison with a first or earlier house.

runs.text: meira em comparação dalgũa feita de nouo.

lines.note: Meira completes primeira: the earlier house in comparison with one newly built. Preserve the printed nasal abbreviation in dalgũa.
Kyuutai is old moss, furui koke. The scan restores the vowel in Furui and shows no comma between Muſgo and velho; the age phrase continues below.
Muito tempo completes the moss description, moss of long standing. This remains a separate physical continuation.
Kyuutat is reaching completion or perfection, kiwame tassuru. The terminal t and the full Japanese verb are recoverable; the Portuguese continues acabar across the break.
Completes acabar and adds fulfilment, as of a desire. Comprir is retained as printed; the terminal S is the upright written-register label.
Kyuuu is sudden rain, niwakana ame, with murasame as the alternative. The scan restores the damaged headword and both Japanese explanations; Chu- begins chuua.
Ua completes chuua repentina, sudden rain. The historical Portuguese spelling is preserved rather than changed to chuva.
Kyuuon is an old kindness or favour, furuqi megumi. The scan restores megumi and Beneficios; an- continues into antiguos below.
Tiguos completes antiguos: favours or benefits received long ago. The next entry shifts from old favours to an old dwelling.
Kyuusei concerns long residence, furuqu sumu. The scan supports the adverbial Furuqu and the verb ſumu, while Habitação restores the damaged Portuguese noun.
Kyuusei sarigatashi says that one is reluctant to leave an old home. The Portuguese starts from the place where someone has lived; hũ is the printed nasal abbreviation, not hã.

runs.text: morou muito tempo aparta ſe com difficuldade.

lines.note: A person who has lived in a place a long time leaves it with difficulty. Aparta ſe is retained with the printed separation.

Kyuusen is literally yumiya, bows and arrows, glossed here as warfare. The example repeats the headword with abbreviated final nasal ẽ before the physical line break; that letter is roman, not italic.
Kyuusen ni tazusawaru means being engaged in military matters. The scan supports plural couſas at the right edge rather than the draft singular.
Completes the warfare translation, then begins kyuusen wo moppara ni suru, devoting oneself to warfare. The scan restores guerra and xenuo; a visible terminal hyphen divides ſu- from ru below.
Ru completes suru, and Idem refers back to being occupied with warfare. The short line is not a separate lexical entry.
Kyuuseki is an old trace, furuqi ato. The Portuguese is Raſto, ou ſinal que, a trace or sign that remains; both nouns correct substantial OCR damage.
The continuation describes an old surviving trace or place. Preserve the somewhat compressed printed syntax and the final &c. instead of rewriting the definition into modern Portuguese.
Kyuushin is an old retainer, furuqi shinka. The damaged Japanese explanation reads xinca, not xine; Portuguese criado antiguo confirms a person who has long served.
Kyuushit denotes an old house, furuqi ie. Caſa corrects the OCR Coſa; final t in the Japanese headword is retained.
The next kyuushit denotes a palace, miya no ie. The full royal-title gloss is italic; the OCR split the final y from its word and typeface.
Kyuusho is an old writing, furuqi kakimono. Liuro gives the book sense; enlarged right-edge inspection confirms eſcri-, including the small i and terminal mark, before tura below.
Tura completes eſcritura antigua, an old writing or document. This closes the preceding book entry.
Kyuushu is a former lord or master, furuqi aruji. The scan restores both the Japanese phrase and the Portuguese antiguo; the corrupted draft obscured their matching sense.
Kyuushuu is explained as kokonotsu no kuni, nine provinces or realms. The final u has a length mark; the Portuguese plural reinos is fully visible.
Do Ximo locates the nine realms in the western region designated Ximo. Ximo is a Japanese geographical term embedded in Portuguese and retains its observed italic type.
The phrase kyuushu rengyoo is glossed as long-standing practice or exercise. The full Portuguese restores several OCR omissions; no modern technical interpretation is inserted into the transcription.
Kyuuyen is explained by hato and tsubame, pigeons and swallows. The scan restores the ampersand and the t of tçubame; the divided an has no securely visible terminal hyphen.
Dorinhas completes andorinhas, swallows. It is one continuous printed fragment, not the OCR do inhas.

Kyuuyoo is urgent business, isogi no yoo. The damaged double-s sort in Neceßidade is read as beta-like; the heavily inked terminal mark after ne is retained as a hyphen before negocio on the next row.
Gocio completes negocio, urgent business. The apparent paragraph sign in the draft is not part of this body line; the separate lower-right Qi... belongs to page furniture.
Abraded catchword read as Qiǔ, anticipating Qiǔyǔ at the opening of f403. The residual feet and upper mark of the final vowel are faint; the expansion to the complete next headword is not supplied.
